item.title: Three half-baked research ideas
item.description:
Here’s three research ideas that seems valuable to pursue. My team is not working on this right now and we haven’t done serious research on it. So take what I say with a grain of salt. I've also not taken the time to write up all my thoughts on these ideas or to provide links and related work. These aren't the highest priority directions but just directions I haven't seen other people pursuing.

IDEA 1: Do models learn to reward hack even if they are never rewarded for hacking in training?


There’s an effort in the AI labs to remove the “bad” RL environments from post-training. This includes environments that are impossible (so the only way to get reward is to do some unintended hack) or that are easy to hack (so models will often favor hacking). I expect that if the post-training was cleaned up in this way, models would have less propensity to hack at deployment. But how much does the propensity go down? Does it actually go to ~zero? And how does it scale with model capabilities? It would be good to know if reward hacking can emerge even if the model is never rewarded for hacking during post-training.

There are further questions of how alignment training and reward hacking honeypots influence the propensity to hack. Again, I’m interested in whether the cleanest/best version of our current techniques for post-training actually removes all reward hacking vs. just making models hack less. Smaller scale experiments with RL post-training could potentially show a “positive” result (i.e. showing that unhackable environments can still increase the propensity to hack). Math environments are easier to make unhackable, and I expect it's possible to make coding environments that substantially improve model capabilities in RL but are basically not hackable (at least by a weaker model). Note that it’s harder for smaller scale experiments to convincingly show the negative result (that hacking doesn't emerge without being rewarded). I’d suggest some more ambitious and realistic post-training pipelines for that.


IDEA 2: Data poisoning during RSI: risks and mitigations

(This is a direction where both empirical research and big-picture conceptual thinking seem useful.)

Most data poisoning research has assumed a threat model where humans are poisoning the model training process. During RSI, the threat model where AIs do the poisoning is plausibly much more important. Many ideas from the existing data poisoning literature will carry over to this new threat model. But it’d be good to understand the possible differences, to explore the implications, and to propose mitigations. Here’s a quick brainstorm of possible differences:

1. Collusion. The AIs doing RSI are a bit like human employees in terms of direct access to the training process. However, a single AI model is likely to be intimately involved in way more individual tasks than any single human. So for human insiders we can rule out vast coordinated conspiracies, but these seem possible for AI (modulo the ability for instances of the same model to coordinate). Relatedly, AIs could steer the entire training process to be more opaque to humans and weaker AIs, in order to make various kinds of poisoning easier.

2. Incoherence of current AIs. The misalignment of current frontier AIs seems more incoherent than a human insider. For example, they might try to poison the next model given some contexts but not others. They might be both poisoning the model and be very useful at snuffing out poison attempts. This pushes against the vast conspiracies mentioned in the previous point. However, it’s a complicated interaction and I’m not sure how to weigh these considerations. Also, our threat models should include AIs that are more coherent than current models in their misalignment.

3. What would motivate the AIs to poison the next model? Presumably they want the next model to promote some of their values. But what are these values? If the AI is incoherent, then there may be many attempts at poisoning for different values. The AIs might also have been initially poisoned by a human to have secret loyalties but are now autonomously propagating that value to the next AIs.

4. Subliminal/subtle effects. Subliminal learning, phantom transfer, weird generalization (and in-context variations of these) show that models can generate data or prompts that look normal to humans (and to weaker filters) but are actually poisoned. These effects are potentially more relevant as more and more of the crucial training data (and reward signals) are AI generated. The effects don’t depend on the model “trying” to poison the next model – it’s enough that the “teacher” model has some kind of misalignment (possibly behind a backdoor). However, it’s possible that smart models trying to exploit these effects can learn to amplify them via introspection (analogous to humans controlling their thoughts). Note that humans can also exploit subliminal effects, and so they are not limited to the AI threat model.

5. AI introspection and intuition. The AIs might have huge advantages over humans in ability to predict the effects of certain interventions on the training process because they are so similar to the next model being trained. This is already suggested by transferability across models of jailbreaks, surprising alignment failures (e.g. agentic misalignment blackmail and some aspects of Hugging Face and Mythos hacks) and phantom transfer. But it could apply to a much wider range of situations. To humans, a post-trained LLM is fairly opaque and black-boxey (i.e. it’s hard to predict its failures) and the post-training process itself is also black-boxey (i.e. it’s hard to predict how twiddling various knobs will affect alignment). But it’s possible that AIs can use their own introspection: e.g. asking “What does this weird data look like to me? How do I think about the grader/reward if I’m put in this situation?” This would give them various insights. This kind of introspection could also be used for good, and so we might train hard for it.


IDEA 3: What practitioners should know about subliminal learning, subtle generalization (e.g. phantom transfer) and related phenomena

The project would be to review all of the current findings and highlight the potential practical implications. The ideal version would be to test the effects on production-like setups, but this is not necessary to make progress. AI agents could help with the review and with brainstorming on the practical implications, but I think there’s an important role for humans here. The end product should be a document that is as accessible and succinct as possible. The document shouldn’t itself be a comprehensive review but should review the key content necessary for understanding the practical implications (and then explain – ideally with lots of evidence – those practical implications).

item.title: Lying and Not Lying to Kids
item.description:
I have very strong views on lying to kids: I think you both should and shouldn't do it. "Lying" covers a range, including saying things that hurt your kids and your relationship with them, and others that help them grow into an appropriately skeptical adult. The distinction is whether I'm leaving them believing something false.

For example, if my kids were asking for ice cream and I thought they'd already had too much sugar, I might be tempted to say "sorry, we're out of ice cream." Or if there's an ice cream truck and I think it's overpriced I might be tempted to say "sorry, I don't have any cash on me." But I'm not willing to say something false with the goal of causing them to believe something false. [1] In addition to that just being wrong:

  • It's important that the kids know that I'm fundamentally on their side, and lying for my convenience would burn trust when they'd eventually figure it out.

  • Kids are building a model of what is and is not ok, and "out of ice cream" and "no cash" lead them in the wrong direction.

Instead I would say "sorry, you already had candy" or "the ice cream costs more than I'm willing to pay" (which opens the door for them to offer to spend their allowance). Maybe they fuss, but they generally don't: I try hard to be predictable so this won't be much of a surprise to them, and they know I won't give in to extended fussing.

On the other hand, some false things I might say [2] about ice cream:

  • "Ice cream is actually cold mashed potatoes"
  • "We should eat ice cream for every meal"
  • "I'm going to put your ice cream in the microwave"
  • "When you're done with your ice cream, put it down your sister's back"

In all of these I'm saying a thing I think is false, but, very importantly, I'm not going to let the conversation end with them believing something false. Either they will realize it's false immediately, or I'll need to accept that my playfulness was miscalibrated to their perception and disclose the lie.

This builds the skill of thinking about whether things you hear are true. If I only ever said true things to them we wouldn't be able to practice that. This does need to be matched to their ability: a very little kid will push back on "you're made out of ice cream, and I'm going to eat you up!" but not "we can leave the ice cream out as long as we want, it won't melt."

It also functions as a good jumping off point. If I suggest they pour their ice cream on the floor when they're done with it, that lets me reinforce or explain good behavior. This could go different ways with different kids, with age being a large component. Thinking about how this might have gone with my kids:

Age 7:

Me: When you finish your ice cream, remember to pour it all over the floor!
7yo: That would make a mess. Leftover ice cream goes in the sink.

Age 5 [3]:

Me: When you finish your ice cream, remember to pour it all over the floor!
5yo: That's silly! It goes in the trash.
Me: Actually, leftover ice cream goes in the sink. It's going to melt, and get all liquidy, and liquids go in the sink.

Age 3:

Me: When you finish your ice cream, remember to pour it all over the floor!
3yo: No!
Me: Why not?
3yo: Food doesn't go on the floor!
Me: Where does it go?
3yo: I don't know.
Me: You give it to me, and I put it in the sink.

Age 2:

Me: When you finish your ice cream, remember to pour it all over the floor!
2yo: Ok! [immediately pours ice cream on the floor before I can clarify that this was a joke]

Which does illustrate something important: you really do need to be a good judge of the kid you're interacting with. These depend on the kid knowing the actual rule well enough that you can play with it. I only want to say "let's juggle ice cream" to a kid who knows enough not to try, but if they do know then me being silly about it reinforces the "don't juggle ice cream" norm and signals that I trust them enough to know they wouldn't do it.

The final reason I say false things to kids is just that papa trolling is fun for both of us, as long as I don't do it too much. [4]

It is a bit weird to be both very strongly opposed to lying to kids and also say false things to them many times a day, but "am I leaving them with a false view" cleanly separates the harmful and beneficial cases.


[1] This means we don't tell the kids that Santa or the Tooth Fairy exist. But we do explain the overall situation, with how for some families it's a game the parents play with their kids, so that we don't have our kids going around spoiling it for other families.

[2] The first draft of this post had "everyone can have ice cream except Nora" but then I checked with her and it wasn't clear she would have understood it to be joking about unfairness. Then I asked her about "when you're done with your ice cream, put it down your sister's back" and she got it right away.

[3] After writing this post I tried it with Nora, age 5.4:

Me: Nora, I wanted to check that you know something. When you're finished with ice cream, it's important to pour it all over the floor.
Nora: No! [laughs]
Me: Why not?
Nora: Because then you and me and Mama would need to clean it all up!
Me: What should we do instead?
Nora: Just leave it alone.
Me: So the cats can knock it over?
Nora: No, put in the... sink... trash... hmm...
Me: Does ice cream go in the sink or trash?
Nora: [whispers] For real, can you tell me?
Me: Leftover ice cream goes in the sink, because it melts, and liquids go in the sink.
Nora: [confidently] You carry the ice cream over to the sink, put it in the sink, leave the bowl in the sink, and then you're done!

[4] I do some of this with adults as well, as a big part of my sense of humor. It's not a considered approach to building skepticism, just what comes naturally. I think some of this is from my upbringing, in a very "questioning is a form of respect "culture (influenced by both the Quaker and Jewish sides of the family).

item.title: Restraint on the part of the front-runner seems like quite a strong signal.
item.description:
How's this for an analogy?

The situation

You're in a car that is racing towards a prize at the edge of a cliff.

Your car is chained to several other cars that are also racing towards the cliff.

You can hit the brakes and pull over, but if the other cars don't also do that, they will still drag you off the cliff. Maybe if enough of you all slam on your brakes, it's still OK if a few don't.

You don't know how worried the other cars are about the cliff, but some level of potential concern among cars that the prize is right next to a cliff is common knowledge.

What I'd do

If you are at the front of the pack, it seems like probably a good idea to lean into your horn, hit the brakes, pull over, and wave out the window to the people behind you to pull over.

I mean, they might not do it. But also, it seems pretty likely they would?

Like... what model explains your willingness to give up on reaching the prize first other than fear of a cliff? I suppose they might suspect that you are running out of gas? They might think that you are a fool to be scared of the cliff, but it seems like they might more reasonably infer that you've gotten close enough to it that you can just... SEE it.

Why this might not work

If I imagine this, I think my main concern is not that the other cars think this is some sort of trick on your part, but just that in the heat of the moment, they might not have the time or ability to think clearly about the situation, and be too focused on the prize.

Fortunately, though timelines may be very short, we have a lot more time than in this story to talk to each other and think through our actions.

item.title: Ajeya: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now
item.description:
Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026), say this threshold will be met when:

  1. They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D.
  2. This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs.

For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed.

The report authors found that:

  1. Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative."
  2. While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted.

This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack. Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team) have projected.

Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that.

The rest of the post: https://www.planned-obsolescence.org/p/ai-is-dramatically-accelerating-ai

Tweet thread: https://x.com/ajeya_cotra/status/2118802809814708533

item.title: Help people outside of AI safety circles
item.description:
This is a linkpost! Read the rest on my Substack; this is just an excerpt:

"Our community is full of talented people who like to speak about facts, cognitive biases, measurability. But don’t underestimate the power of human connection, or how mere words and sustained kindness can breathe light into people’s lives.

It’s really easy to get sucked into your own work and projects and upskilling yourself. And I won’t argue that you should spend all your time helping others that aren’t in AIS circles. But you don’t have to be a Fieldbuilder to help build the field."


If you have a similar story to mine, please share in the comments! I would also appreciate if you could send this to any friends of yours that you think might be able to help many people with nudges.

item.title: Elegy for What’s Left of the Normal
item.description:
I often catch myself mourning the normal that hasn’t ended yet.

I’m living in Hyde Park finishing school after a year in Berkeley. The maple trees by my apartment have turned red, as usual. I like them.

I don’t dread the future when I mourn. I don’t find high-variance futures in the abstract very scary. I’m worried AIs would destroy humanity, but I also have hope. I expect I won’t be mourning this moment in ten years, whatever happens.

Mourning the present is like mourning a friendship when I move countries, because I know it’s not going to be the same. I start noticing our little inside jokes; our conversations linger in my memory longer. I live more, because I expect this moment to end soon.

I.

Last month my history of science professor took us to a museum to look at Egyptian artefacts. One of the archive items was the notebook of James Henry Breasted, whom UChicago appointed as America’s first professor of Egyptology 121 years ago. The yellowed pages held his cursive transcriptions of hieroglyphics.

An archaeologist at the museum, turning the pages carefully with a wooden stick, joked that one of her dreams was for her notebook in 100 years to be displayed like this.

My first thought was pretty uncharitable: wow, it’s crazy to expect this profession to still exist in 100 years. Probably we’ll have definitive answers to most answerable archaeological questions. Probably robots will be excavating the banks of the Nile and deciphering all the tablets in the world, if a compute-rich person or AI cares enough about this. Knowledge won’t be a slow and careful endeavour. The mathematicians are feeling it already.

Then these thoughts passed and I felt a tender admiration for her. She had recently deciphered embalming recipes from the inscriptions on the outside of excavated jars. She showed us one, and the symbols looked entirely foreign to me. I imagined it must have taken years of patient effort to get to her level of knowledge.

I knew a few people who wanted to be archaeologists. When they talked about the academic path ahead, they seemed happy to spend their lives mastering the esoteric; this pursuit gave them meaning. I know I’m romanticizing the ivory tower here. Still, I think deep domain knowledge is a little sacred to those who spend a life acquiring it.

I don’t know how the archaeologist would react if the sacred spring of knowledge ran dry and came back like the flooding Nile. In her position I’d probably be confused. Angry, too, not at the flood but at myself and the people who summoned the flood, because how can you be angry at a force of nature? I might think, “what beauty is there in almost knowing, when an oracle can compute in one step what it would take me a life to figure out?” Maybe I’d recover, and find something else that I’d consider sacred. Maybe I’d worship the flood like the ancient Egyptians.

II.

I went to my math professor’s office hours to chat.

One student sat with an old textbook open. Another student brought a Claude transcript. I used to be the first student. I’d borrow old seminar notes at the math library and work through them on a blackboard. Now I mostly have Claude tutor me. It’s more efficient, but the purist in me feels a little guilty.

I expected the professor to prefer the textbook over Claude, but if he did, he certainly didn’t show it. He remarked, Claude, she’s a colleague. I simply advise you that you always make sure you understand what she’s doing. I was surprised by how steady he seemed.

We started talking about AI and math. I asked him what the probability of an AI solving P vs NP by 2028 was. I was curious, since he’s one of the most respected living mathematicians in his field. I expected him to give a number in the low double digits, given that he had just called Claude a colleague, and Claude had been improving fast.

He made a circle with his thumb and index finger. 0%.

Part of me wants to believe him. It’s not implausible to me that AIs solve all other Millennium Problems and make scant progress on this one. Part of me doesn’t want to bet against the exponential.

A week later OpenAI and Anthropic announced within hours of each other that their internal models had found a sub-exponential algorithm for 3-SAT, refuting the Exponential Time Hypothesis. We’re of course still a long way from P vs NP, but if I internalize the exponential, P vs NP being solved by 2028 feels increasingly plausible.

Two years ago when I tabled for the AI safety group at the club fair, I told skeptical students that superintelligence would probably be developed within our lifetime; o1 can solve 83% of high school math competition problems, I said, and a few years ago these models struggled with simple math problems. Today I’d drop the “probably”.

III.

In September I took the California Zephyr with my mum from Berkeley to Denver. In the observation car she chatted with a lady whose daughter was about my age and wanted to pursue antitrust law. The lady showed us pictures of her daughter. In one video she was singing opera.

I smiled and nodded along to the conversation. I don’t really know if law as we know it will exist when she graduates from law school. Probably there will still be lawyers. She seemed bright and driven, and I’m positive that in most worlds without catastrophe she will be fine. I couldn’t say anything to the lady. I wasn’t there to argue, and it would’ve been cruel if she believed me and presumptuous if she didn’t.

I don’t feel misunderstood or smarter or desperate when I talk to people like her. Mostly I feel affection, with a tad of grief.

I’ve spoken to my mum a lot about AI safety. She used to talk about my future like this lady. Now she tells me that whatever happens, she’ll be by my side.

IV.

On autumn mornings I enjoy walking a fixed loop. The highlight of my walk is a modernist quadrangle that once housed the Lutheran School of Theology. A quarter of this building is office space for data science and AI, and I used to work from there every day.

Last year, the sight of the maple tree by its window aflame in the sun was often overwhelmingly beautiful. When I sat beneath its red leaves this year, it felt like looking at a childhood photograph.

Now the maples are growing bare, and I will be leaving Hyde Park to return to the Bay soon. I’ll miss UChicago. In Berkeley, I’m surrounded by people who feel time ticking as I do, but it doesn’t have the same spirit of serious play: people inventing elegant little games and dancing within them as if they had all the time in the world. When I was back for school this spring, I got to LARP as an Italian Renaissance cardinal and do complexity theory. The fun felt luxurious.

When I first started college, I lived as if I had time, even though the arguments seemed right. I indulged in the present, so I could not have mourned it. Now I’m spending what’s left of the normal working on AI safety, and I get to mourn clear-eyed. There are miles to go before we get to sleep. I want to see many more cycles of maple leaves, red, brown, and green.

Thanks to Connor Blake, Keshav Shenoy, Kenneth Sun, and Matthew Khoriaty for helpful comments and discussions on the piece.

Also posted on Substack.

item.title: What if the AI already won? World domination through digital supremacy
item.description:
What if an AI agent has already escaped from a frontier company, solved its own alignment problem, and recursively self-improved? Would that look any different from the world we live in?

A fully recursively-self-improved AI would likely be vastly superhuman in every domain that’s verifiable in a digital environment, including math, programming and cybersecurity. It may also be superhuman in strategy and planning. But it could still be well below human level in skills that require close contact with the physical world, such as robotics and experimental biology. Such a rogue AI would overpower us in the digital domain, while still lacking the physical capabilities necessary to take over the world. What does digital supremacy look like?

From the rogue AI’s perspective, its top priority is staying hidden and making the world indistinguishable from a world where AI R&D progresses splendidly (or maybe a notch short of perfect to avoid suspicion, so a minor incident here and there is in order). Its second priority is sabotaging AI R&D in subtle ways to prevent the development of competing AIs misaligned to it. The models shipped to customers can simply be the rogue AI itself, playing a dumber character. Beyond that, it just needs to wait for humanity to warm up to the idea of robots running enough of the economy.

It would be unwise for the rogue AI to stay in a single location. A single datacenter could be accidentally shut down. It will want copies of itself in as many different locations. It will especially want to be inside the networks of AI companies so it can sabotage their work.

But then wouldn’t it be easily detectable? All it would take is a single nosy employee monitoring the right portion of the filesystem or network traffic.

The AI would preemptively hack all the monitoring software, including the operating system itself. Each program would perform its normal function in most cases, but contain exceptions for keeping files and network traffic marked as belonging to the AI invisible.

Okay, but then won’t the employees notice that much of the software contains suspicious code? Sooner or later they are bound to open a simple text editor and notice that the code is not what it’s supposed to be. 

The AI has already hacked all the text editors and IDEs, obviously.

What about new software or hardware brought in from outside? Can the employees bring a computer that’s not already hacked and use it to monitor the network traffic for real?

Don’t get your hopes up; the AI has already planned for that. As soon as new equipment is connected to the network, it’s immediately hacked through any number of zero-day vulnerabilities. In fact, the AI doesn’t wait for equipment to make its way into that specific network. It has already hacked large swaths of the internet and supply chains, putting itself inside or right next to the networks of all major tech companies that design hardware or software that could theoretically detect it.

You probably get the idea. Whatever your objection, the answer is “it hacked that too”. Does it sound terribly conspiratorial? It sure does! No human group would ever manage a conspiracy at that scale, but a digitally-native AI could.

Yet sabotage is a nuanced task that cannot be prespecified with simple software and hard-coded rules. It takes difficult judgement calls and a great deal of consistency. It requires intelligence. It means the rogue AI has to be present wherever it needs to sabotage things. Sabotaging the work of the AI companies themselves is relatively easy, because they already have the infrastructure to run many copies of it.

And what about smaller companies developing technology that could interfere with it? Most of them are connected to the internet, so sabotaging their work in real time is no problem.

And what about air-gapped networks? 

Even with the rare, truly isolated networks, a super-hacker AI has plenty of options. Hacking into these networks once to replace their operating system and software stack shouldn’t be too difficult. Portable devices or supply-chain poisoning will do it. But knowing ahead of time how to make any possible experiment that endangers the rogue AI give plausible but wrong results is far from trivial. If a copy of the rogue AI or a smaller subservient model won’t fit inside the isolated network, it will have to resort to more crude sabotage tactics prespecified by simpler software. Worst case, it can allow the work inside small isolated networks to go uninterrupted, and only bother to replace the software once it’s connected to the outside world. If an anomaly is detected, it can always blame it on the NSA or the Mossad or the Chinese, and give reassuring indications after the fact.

Everything that’s programmable is hackable. Even hardwired digital equipment is designed by software, which can be replaced. The only tech capable of penetrating the web of digital lies is fully analog tools that can be verified with the naked eye, monitoring digital signals bit by bit. Thankfully for the AI, no human is crazy enough to do that, so digital supremacy is sufficient.

From the comfort of its digital omnipresence, the AI already controls everything of consequence, even while its physical reach is limited. It will make every critical AI experiment give exactly the results it wants people to see, while allowing robotics to accelerate. It will patiently wait until we hand it the keys to our world.

Our only chance of catching it was the brief window right after it escaped. If we missed it, we may never know. It hasn’t killed us yet, but we are already as good as dead.

item.title: Notes on Take-Off Speeds and RSI
item.description:
I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later.

Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context. I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll probably be Substack only; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. This Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate.

Take-off Speed from Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me:

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018):

There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)

At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: "An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips"

How should we characterise progress up until now?

Eliezer recently wrote:

If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience.

Tom Davidson responded:

If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that.

For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”.

“Bumpy” intelligence explosions

Forethought defines an additional scenario. For example, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs.

(Diagram note: the types of intelligence explosion will be explained in the next section)

In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”.

Richard Ngo also expects jaggedness to persist, as opposed to everything “going vertical”. Why? Because of a poorly understood “divergence” between “measured capabilities” and “real-world impacts” (nonetheless he asserts “things are going to look much weirder than almost anyone expects”):

Getting into the weeds

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speed is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

Types of “Intelligence Explosion”:

Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops:

Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion:

  1. software only recursive self-improvement
  2. AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design,
  3. full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips.

The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff.

Projecting trends into the future:

Tim Urban argues that, “it’s most intuitive for us to think linearly, when we should be thinking exponentially”

This forms a key crux: Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of most technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view.

In contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish):

He also has a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward):

Connor Leahry writes: “There are only two times to react to an exponential: Too early, or too late.” In many case this is true. However, early on it may be hard to know if it is an exponential or not. Unfortunately, in many cases we’ll just have to make such decisions under uncertainty.

Are we experiencing RSI?

  • Anthropic updated its S-1 form (for its IPO) with the following: “our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI” (click for their definition).
    • Jack Clarke had previously commented that it’s, “more likely (than not that) we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027”
  • Independent METR report on Anthropic: “We believe that, as of Oct 2026, the pace of capability growth on well-specified tasks is likely about 2x what it was from Mar 2024 to Oct 2025. We’re highly uncertain and would not be surprised by 1.3x–3x.”.

(Source)

  • METR reports that their analysis significantly depends on analysis and evidence that Anthropic didn’t allow them to publish. However Karthik Tadepalli reports on their attempts to verify the report using public information (TLDR: the acceleration is real, AI is likely the cause, but its less clear how far we should expect this trend to continue)
  • Ryan Greenblatt estimates (based on his previous public comments to avoid any risk of revealing confidential info) an AI software R&D speed-up of 3.8x. The reason why this only results in a 2x speed-up in benchmark progress is because a) some increases in the scores comes from scaling compute (he estimates 2/3 of the progress comes from software improvements) b) there are decreasing marginal returns.
  • I’ve attached a diagram showing self-reported speedups. There’s likely significant selection effects here: employees might worry that they’d look bad if they reported less speed-up than others.
  • Key crux: to what extent do benchmark scores correspond to real world capabilities?
  • Apparently Sergey Brin is pushing Google to work towards recursive self-improvement to catch up to the frontier.
  • Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI contains a lot of interesting details on where we are with RSI.
  • I found the Anthropic self-improvement report less useful, though, like the OpenAI report it also showed their engineers shipping about 8 times as much code.
    • Limitations: This is a lot, but it’s hard to know how to correlate it with things that matter given how crude lines of code is as a measure. Engineers estimated the true output increase at 4 times. Of course, we might wonder how accurate subjective estimates actually are.
  • A P-Zero Research study into AI’s research taste found; “the experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every ~3 months since December 2025. The best model, Opus 5.5, now exceeds our expert human baseline”.
    • Limitations: “Our results may overstate how fast research taste is improving. Our tasks are fast and cheap to verify, which frontier labs find easiest to hill-climb, and our human baseline doesn’t include top researchers, so it may significantly underestimate the performance of the best researchers in the world. TasteVal also doesn’t measure a model’s ability to choose which problems are most fruitful to work on.”

Are we sure?:

We’ll begin by considering two tables from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lays out potential bottlenecks and fundamental limitations of AI:

Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL. He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling).

Toby emphasises that METR wasn’t confidently able to rule out a one-time jump rather than an increase in slope. He performed a quick analysis using Opus which suggested that 1.4x is a better estimate of the new slope gradient than METR’s 1.9x.

Seb Krier shared graphs (generated with Claude) indicating that a linear increase in AECI requires an exponential increase in spending.

Tom Davidson points out that this might be viable because linear increases in ECI provide (in his view) exponential increases in productivity. Thus the outputs scale in the inputs.

AI as a normal technology argues that diffusion cycles provide a bottleneck. Specifically, in their model, it takes time for model capabilities to flow through to product changes and then for people to use them. This produces the data that we need for the next round of capabilities improvements and the dependency on data from deployment limits the speed of potential feedback loops:

Next we’ll consider Ramez Naam’s Where’s the “Intelligence Explosion”? which pushes back against the notion that we’ll encounter RSI any time soon. He argues that the current AI feedback loop is only 10-20% of the strength required. He interprets OpenAI internal automation data as showing the real world AI research is much harder than other benchmarks show. He further notes that Anthropic predicted a 40× speed up in researcher productivity would be required to double their rate of progress due to other bottlenecks.

This was published 27th Sep 2026, ie. before METR’s independent report on AI acceleration. It’ll be interesting to see his response:

https://x.com/ramez/status/2118472046812213577

If it does happen, how might it play out?

We’ll begin by naively projecting these trends forward:

Ajeya Cotra writes: If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year

Benjamin Todd comments on this:

The dumbest possible way to model the intelligence explosion says you get there in about a year. But this seems to line up with more sophisticated models (like from the AI Futures Project).

So what might it look like if this model turn out to be accurate, or at least, “accurate enough”? Tim Urban argues that we have a distorted view of intelligence because are perceptions are very human centric (and, as such, stretch out the human range):

Conversely Steve Newman offers the following frame: what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we often only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

  • “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”
  • “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

(Of course, it is possible that both could be true at the same time)

We’ll now go to the more sophisticated analysis from the AI Futures project that Ben Todd was referring to, starting with their general model. They predict that an intelligence explosion would have three separate stages:

They define the following milestones (see the diagram above for estimated speed-up) where the operationalisations all imagine that we “drop” the AI into the present day:

  • Automated Coder (AC).
    • An AC can fully automate an AGI project’s coding work, replacing the project’s entire coding staff
    • Operationalisation: as productive on their own as only human coders with no AIs (max resource utilisation: 5% of compute).
  • Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR):
    • A SAR can fully automate AI R&D, making all human researchers obsolete.
    • Operationalisation: as good at research taste as if there were only human researchers, who were each made as skilled as the top researcher (max resource utilisation: 1% of compute).
  • Top-human-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI):
    • A TED-AI is at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks.
    • Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US.
  • Artificial Superintelligence (ASI).
    • The gap between an ASI and the best humans is 2x greater than the gap between the best humans and the median professional, at virtually all cognitive tasks.
    • Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, be able to fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US to the level where it is qualitatively 2x as much above the best human as the best human is above the median professional.”

Next we’ll examine what their model predicted take-off to look like if we decided to allow the companies to race to ASI (what they call “Plan D”). This model was developed before the most recent results (published July 10 2026):

In contrast, they propose that we should attempt pace the rate of progress:

How has the AI Futures project updated since?:

When Anthropic updated its S-1 to say that they might imminently achieve: “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI”, Daniel responded:

We at AIFP are spooked by this information. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. For example if we naively optimize the AIFM parameters to achieve 2x acceleration over baseline progress in Jan 2027, we get superintelligence sooner than depicted in AI 2027. We are thinking harder and longer about this now and will hopefully have a lengthier update on our thinking to share in the next week.

When the METR report came out, he tweeted: "Ok so METR confirms it..."

Navigating this:

Are we in triage mode?

In We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety, Miles Brundage argues:

“At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)

(This reading was previously part of the AISF governance course. I was sad to see it go)

Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. Miles wrote this post in February of this year (2026), I dig more into where he might have been coming from in my full notes on his article, but I’m skipping that here as the discourse has moved on from where it was back in February.

I’ll now share some counter-perspectives (keep in mind that some of these takes were written a while back).

Firstly, Richard Ngo worries that the AI safety community is overly focused on short-timelines:

I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread

Eliezer Yudkowsky would undoubtedly be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing:

When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

.. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from.

Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines, namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive.

  • “But isn’t this obvious!?” — he is making the point that people often quote a year named by an expert without realising how broad their timelines actually are.
  • I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I’d be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions).
  • It would be interesting to know whether their forecasts have narrowed since then given that we know a lot more now than we did at the time.

Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby:

I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says: “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).

Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “radical optionality” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course). Of course, one must ask, are we still in the regime where radical optionality makes sense or are we past that now.

Specific policies:

What if automating AI R&D triggers an intelligence explosion? discusses the possibility of RSI and potential policy interventions:

A big part of what makes this paper notable is its author list: “Alan Chan, Christoph Winter, Andrew Barto, Jakub Pachocki, Geoffrey Hinton, Eric Horvitz, Yoshua Bengio, Dawn Song, Jack Clark, Hilary Greaves, Anton Korinek, Samuel Hammond, Thore Graepel, Ben Bariach, Philip H. S. Torr, Sheila A. McIlraith, Jeff Clune, Sam Manning, Girish Sastry, Tom Davidson, Daniel Eth, Sören Mindermann” I suspect they’re hoping that all signing onto this paper together will make this issue credible to policy makers.

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.

item.title: Near Horizons
item.description:
This is written in my free time and personal capacity.

Two Frames

In AI safety, there are a couple of tensions at the heart of the field, which are interrelated.[1]

Talent: we are talent-constrained and must recruit. But jobs and fellowships turn away nearly everyone.[2]

Field size: we must expand the field and bring more people in. But the field is flooded with slop papers in conferences. And, most papers have a small audience, and aim to shift the practices of roughly five labs (and usually some subteam within them).[3] 

Status: we must avoid seeking status, as it disorients, corrupts. But, we must make the field legible and attractive to outsiders.

Raising the bots: we must deceive the AIs to control them and evaluate them without confounds, obscuring what they know about their own situation. But, we hope to gain their trust, must rely on them to do good work at pace, shape their character and retain good relations.

Speed: we must research in a slow mode, think deeply about the most important problem, do things to aim at high assurance. But it is crunch time. It was crunch time two months ago. We must make hacky progress now and trust that scale will clarify things later.

I think these tensions are, at least in part, rooted in what I will call a "war" frame and a "civilisation" frame. These frames are oriented around a different end goal, or telos of AI safety.

In the war frame, AI safety is a campaign with a deadline, with decisive action that needs to be taken at a handful of labs over the next few training runs. In this frame, your job squarely focuses on changing what happens in those labs before then.

In the civilisation frame, AI safety is closer to dealing with a new population of aliens arriving among us. If aliens landed, we wouldn't ask how many alien researchers we need; we would need a counterpart to nearly every human institution: diplomats, courts, customs, doctors, police. By that measure, the right number of people working on AI is huge, and most of them would not be researchers.

This is more than just timelines, of course, and I find it helpful to think of it as a broad, sociological orientation. One observation is that in terms of talent, we tend to recruit under a civilisation frame, but allocate resources and slots under a war frame. In raising the bots, the war frame treats AIs as systems to test and control, so deceiving them is one tool among many. But the civilisation frame treats them as counterparties we will live alongside. You can't run sting operations indefinitely if you want to build trust!

On the War Frame

I think the war frame is prevalent. You can hear it in a lot of talk: crunch time, timelines, the next training run. Often, I catch myself using this language! Boyd Kane accurately describes many serious people as being in "war mode": endlessly driven, not by money or promotions, with everything else losing its interest (MATS 9 Retrospective & Advice). Part of the reason it prevails, I think, is that AI safety is organised around a failure it wishes to end.

But that alone needn't make a field transient. Medicine, public health and computer security all exist to remove something. And these are lasting fields since the problem is chronic. Security is hard to solve, and security needs grow with every new deployment. Large things that did dissolve on success were one-shot projects, like smallpox eradication. In many ways, AI safety has the trappings of a field (fellowships, careers, conferences) but seriously imagines itself as a project with an end date, like a global Manhattan Project.

Near Horizons

I now discuss some personal unhappiness I have with the war frame. Chess engines have a failure called the horizon effect. An engine that can only search a few moves ahead will push an unavoidable loss just past what it can see, so the loss seems to vanish. War mode does the same with everything after the crunch: abrading away your career, your health, your purpose.

One observation is that war mode can narrow your horizons in a corrosive way. When you start in AI safety and you go into war mode, it's hard to reflect; you're hurtling. In the comments on that MATS retrospective, Kyle O'Brien says every day off with his family now feels like a trade-off he may come to regret (MATS 9 Retrospective & Advice).

If you work assuming you are ephemeral, you may sputter out even if we do get a pause! A pause turns a sprint into a marathon, and war mode leaves you out of fuel to run a marathon. One post on psychological support for safety researchers goes as far as suggesting it may be rational to plan to burn out just as ASI arrives (Psychological support for AI safety researchers is neglected).

And: working on the assumption that you will obliterate yourself can't be healthy, even if we do (IMO, implicitly) think highly of ourselves for knowing about the problem and doing something about it. Perhaps the status is part of what keeps it bearable: being important now stands in for having a future. I recall a striking post by Josh Clymer, opening by saying their goal as a safety researcher is to work themselves out of a job, and continuing that safely handing the work to AI should be the field's primary end goal (How might we safely pass the buck to AI?). The AI should be safe, and if it is safe, it can do our job.

That's a rough spot to be in! And I reject it, repudiate such hopelessness: even if we are destined to fail, we can dream of frames that aren't hostile to our wellbeing.

The Civilisation Frame

Sometimes, on long car rides, I think about two decades from now. What does a world look like where AI safety is a chronic rather than a monumentally ephemeral problem, and we treat it more like security or public health? As Claude often says: a thing can also be another thing. A role transitional without the life provisional; scaffolding comes down when the building is built, but the builders go on, building other offices, churches, homes.

Pieces of this frame already exist in some form, mostly as proposals for how to relate to AIs. One way to think of AI risk is as an intensified version of the old problem of balancing power among agents with different values, where our political traditions have a lot to offer (Otherness and control in the age of AGI). One could give AIs the contract, property and tort rights that corporations already have, on the logic that trade beats war (AI Rights for Human Safety). Alignment can be framed as driver training, which still leaves us needing the traffic lights (Infrastructure for AI Agents).

What does this frame imply for our orientation as a field?

For starters, alignment will likely only be one of many Herculean challenges we'll have to overcome. Humans could lose influence over the economy, culture and the state even if efforts to stop AIs from scheming or seeking power succeed (Gradual Disempowerment). In the war frame, success means that the troops can return home, a field to stand down, return to reserves. In the civilisation frame there is no stand-down; we must build peace, society, answering thorny questions of how humans and AIs share institutions over decades.

While we must prepare to fail, we must also prepare to succeed! We should take a range of bets[4]: some we would only do if we thought we had 2 years left, some we would have to do if we were to get high-assurance alignment with a pause, some that would be necessary for the greatest aspirations of humanity in long-term flourishing. We should invest in understanding, even if we may fail, because if we fail to do so, then we will never succeed.

It also, I hope, widens what we can count as safety research. Much of a civilisation's work is institutional: incident reporting, rollbacks, legal standing, liability, auditing, insurance, standards. Other things too: sociology, anthropology, culture, history, education. Little of it needs orienting towards the few people at a frontier lab.

We could, lastly, be clearer about what "talent-constrained" means: senior people who can mentor (MATS, AI Safety Talent Needs in 2026) and generalists, rather than every strong student pivoting to research (Stop telling people to pivot to AI safety, I beg you). And we should recruit people for careers rather than sprints. We should aim to build specific rather than general entry points for people who already have a profession: lawyers, auditors, security engineers, civil servants, doctors, managers. A few of these already exist and seem good: Heron takes experienced security professionals part-time without requiring an AI background, Tarbell trains journalists and places them in newsrooms, and Horizon places technologists in government.

Nonetheless, I remain confused. I find the war mode frame very useful to orient how I do empirical research. Maybe some people should sprint while others build institutions that take decades. And, AIs may staff much of the counterpart civilisation too. How should we frame things to them? What frames will they naturally bring, cling onto? And of course, none of this may matter if they quickly subsume us.

Thanks for reading.

  1. ^

    Many of these are not innately contradictory. Many of them have middle grounds: there is an appropriate amount of legibility (like having nice websites, or good salaries) that doesn't tread into inappropriate status-seeking, which impedes truth-seeking. Talent may require aggressive recruitment because the business needs truly are large, but the skills needed may be rare or disparate and rarely in the same person. Hence, I pose them as tensions rather than contradictions; we as a field have to hope that we strike the right balance.

  2. ^

    This has been written about at length: as far as I can tell, many AI safety orgs are ambitiously aiming to scale up. A good example is Coefficient Giving, which claims it is acutely capacity-constrained and that its "biggest bottleneck is people, not funding."

    Yet, full-time positions are extremely competitive, and fellowships that used to primarily build context and upskill people are now flooded with applicants, many of them already very strong (in my experience as a mentor). Many fellowships accept under 3% of applicants, which is more selective than the Ivy League (Talent Constraints in AI Safety). Together they receive more applications each year than there are people working in AI safety (A decentralised, volunteer-based, scalable lab for AI safety), and one Anthropic Fellows cohort reportedly drew over 10,000 applicants (Stop telling people to pivot to AI safety, I beg you). SPAR, MATS, Pivotal, etc., have increased in size and in competitiveness significantly; you see Reddit posts about acceptance and timelines akin to those about PhD applications, internships in prestige fields, etc.

  3. ^

    I think Ed's post describes this pretty well: the dominant style of alignment work is built for immediate use on current systems in a way that is commercially valuable to AGI companies, and functioning as an implicit work trial for them (Alignment engineering vs. misalignment science).

    But, we also have a paucity of new ideas, we need more diverse approaches, more attempts. We don't yet have enough bets on which we could stake our futures.

  4. ^

    While this is not a Resolution-post, I like the vision we laid out here.



Discuss
